title: Vidura's boat at the Ganga
hookLine: Bhima carries his family through the dark, and a boat carries them over the Ganga: why Hindus call holy places fords
carry: a tirtha is a crossing to the far shore
tomorrow: what does Bhima do with his anger?

cards: Out of the tunnel, into a forest at night, with a town about to wake behind them. Kunti and her sons are worn out, and the dark is thick. So Bhima picks them all up.

The text sets it out: his mother on his shoulders, the twins against his sides, Yudhishthira and Arjuna held by the hand. He pushes through the trees, carrying his whole family at once. The house is behind them.
They still have to get away.

teach.b: They reach the Ganga, and a man is waiting with a boat. He says Vidura sent him. But anyone could say that.
So he gives a sign: he speaks back words from Vidura's warning on the road, words only Yudhishthira understood. Yudhishthira hears them, and the family gets in. Now look at where it ends: a crossing.
The family goes over the Ganga, from the shore where, in everyone's eyes, they died, to a far bank where no one is looking for them. Hindus have a word for a place like that: tirtha.

It literally means a ford, a crossing place in a river. It's also the word for a holy place of pilgrimage. Haridwar and Varanasi, on the Ganga, are great tirthas, and pilgrims travel there to bathe and pray.
Underneath is an old Hindu picture: life itself is a river to cross.

Samsara, the round of birth and death, is the near shore, and freedom is the far one. A hymn many Hindus sing, Bhaja Govindam, calls samsara the sea so hard to cross, and asks Krishna to keep us safe in it by his grace.
A tirtha is where the far shore feels close. So the boatman carries them over, sends them on with good wishes, and goes back the way he came.
And the Pandavas, dead as far as the world knows, step off on the far bank as people no one is looking for.

how: Hindus go on tirtha yatra, pilgrimage, to holy fords and riverbanks such as Haridwar and Varanasi on the Ganga, to bathe, pray and remember their dead.

o: a boat, like the one waiting at the Ganga
the hidden tunnel under the house's floor
a riddle spoken in a tongue few could follow

p: carries the family through the forest
a ford, and a place of pilgrimage
the round of birth and death, a river to cross

s: Vidura came to the river himself
he sent a man with a boat, who proved himself with Vidura's words.
Bhima carried his mother and all four brothers
the text puts them on his shoulders, at his sides and in his hands.
tirtha, the word for a Hindu pilgrimage place, means a crossing
a ford in a river: a place to cross toward the far shore.

games.q: a friend asks why Hindus travel so far to bathe in the Ganga at places like Haridwar. by today's story, what fits?
o: they're tirthas, crossing places; the river stands for crossing samsara toward the far shore.
the water there is just cleaner than at home.
it's mostly a tradition for tourists now.
games.why: tirtha means a ford. the Pandavas crossed the Ganga to a new life; pilgrims go to the tirthas hoping to come nearer the far shore.

practice: Let the chair or the floor take your whole weight, the way Kunti let Bhima carry her through the dark. If you have water near you, touch a drop to your head, the way pilgrims do at a tirtha.
Bring to mind something you're crossing right now, a move, an ending, a change, and the far bank you hope for. If you pray, ask, as the old hymn does, for grace on the crossing.
If you don't, just picture the far shore, and breathe as if you're already halfway over.

wordCard.voice: Nauka, the boat waiting at the Ganga, its boatman proved trustworthy by repeating Vidura's own hidden words.

orig.note: Sanskrit naukā: a boat; Vidura's last piece of help, waiting at the Ganga.

carryVoice: Your line: a tirtha is a crossing to the far shore. Vidura's boat carried them over. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha Parva (Bhima carries the family through the forest; Vidura's man and the boat on the Ganga)
Bhaja Govindam (attributed to Adi Shankara), the verse 'punarapi jananam': samsara, so hard to cross; protect me, Murari, by your grace
